source.text: ወእምህየ፡ ሖርኩ፡ *ካልአ፡ መካነ፡ ምድር፡ ወአርአየኒ፡ ደብረ፡ እሳት፡ ዘያንበለብል፡ መዐልተ፡ ወሌሊተ።

translation.text: And from there I went to another place of the earth, and he showed me[a] a mountain of fire that blazed day and night.

footnotes.text: The selected Ethiopic says he showed me without naming the person. It describes one mountain; the facing Greek uses a plural and does not silently replace this text.

source.text: ወሖርኩ፡ መንገሌሁ፡ ወ*ነጸርኩ፡ ሰብዐተ፡ አድባረ፡ ክቡራነ፡ ወኵሉ፡ ፩እምነ፡ ፩እንዘ፡ ይትዌለጥ፡ ወአእባነ፡ *ክቡራነ፡ ወሠናያነ፡ ወኵሉ፡ ክቡር፡ ወስቡሕ፡ ራእዮሙ፡ ወሠናይ፡ ገጾሙ፡ ፫መንገለ፡ ጽባሕ፡ ወ*ጽኑዓን፡ ፩ዲበ፡ ፩ወ፫መንገለ፡ ሰሜን፡ ፩ዲበ፡ ፩ወቈላት፡ ዕሙቅ፡ ወጠዋያት፡ *አሐቲ፡ ለአሐቲ፡ ኢይትቃረባ።

translation.text: And I went in that direction and saw seven glorious mountains, each differing from the others, and precious and beautiful stones. All were glorious and splendid in appearance and fair in form. Three were toward the east, firmly set one above another, and three toward the north[a], one above another, with deep and winding ravines[b], none coming near another.

footnotes.text: The selected Ethiopic says north; the facing Greek on printed p.61 says south. The alternatives remain separate witnesses.

Deep, winding ravines follows the Ethiopic. The facing Greek describes deep, rough ravines; an earlier one-valley wording is not adopted. The source stones and final inflection still require exact glyph review.

source.text: ወሳብዕ፡ ደብር፡ ማእከሎሙ፡ ለእሎንቱ፡ ወ*ኖኆሙ፡ ዘይትማሰሉ፡ [ኵሎሙ፡] ከመ፡ መንበረ፡ አትራኖስ፡ ወ*የአውድዎ፡ ዕጸወ፡ መዓዛ።

translation.text: And the seventh mountain was among them; it rose above the others[a], like the seat of a throne[b], and fragrant trees encircled it.

footnotes.text: The printed Ethiopic height expression is difficult and Charles discusses readings and reconstruction in p.61 Greek note13 and Ethiopic notes47–49. The bracketed all is editorially questioned; rose above follows the Greek comparison, not an unquestioned Ethiopic main-text clause.
The mountain is compared with a throne seat; the source does not name an occupant or authorize an embodied deity in the artwork.

source.text: ወሀሎ፡ እምውስቴቶሙ፡ ዕፅ፡ ዘአልቦ፡ *ገሙራ፡ አመ፡ ጼወ*ኒ፡ †ወኢ፩እምውስቴቶሙ፡ ወባዕዳነሂ፡ ዘከማሁ፡ አኮ፤ ይምዕዝ፡ እምኵሉ፡ መዐዛ፡ ወቈጽሉ፡ ወጽጌሁ፡ ወዕፁ፡ ኢይጸመው፡ ለዓለም፡ ወፍሬሁኒ፡ ሠናይ፡ ወፍሬሁሰ፡ ከመ፡ አስካለ፡ በቀለት።

translation.text: And among them was a tree whose scent I had never smelled. None among them, nor any other, was like it[a]. Its fragrance surpassed every fragrance. Its leaves, flowers, and wood never wither, and its fruit is beautiful; its fruit is like a cluster of dates[b].

footnotes.text: This opening comparison smooths a damaged Ethiopic clause marked by a dagger. The facing Greek also uses an emended smelling verb; printed p.61 note16 does not identify this tree as myrrh.
The fruit is compared with a palm fruit cluster. That comparison does not establish the visionary tree as a date palm; the leaves, flowers, wood and fruit are separate clauses.

source.text: ውእተ፡ ጊዜ፡ እቤ፡ ዝንቱ፡ ሠናይ፡ ዕፀ፡ ወ†*ሠናይ፡ ለርእይ፡† ወአዳም፡ ቈጽሉ፡ ወ†ፍሬሁኒ፡† ሞገስ፡ ጥቀ፡ ለርእዩ፡ ገጽ።
source.note: Unapplied selected Charles1906 printed source candidate after a chapter-wide first pass. Newly enlarged PDF98 and100 details plus facing Greek/apparatus page99 must be checked before any approval. No manuscript or human specialist certification.

translation.text: Then I said, “This is a beautiful tree, beautiful to look at[a]; its leaves are lovely, and its fruit[b] is very pleasing to look at.”

footnotes.text: The printed Ethiopic appearance expression is dagger-marked as difficult. In p.62 note9 Charles prefers a Greek fragrance reading; this candidate retains his printed Ethiopic appearance sense.
The printed Ethiopic has fruit, marked with daggers. Charles p.62 note10 proposes flowers with a Greek comparison; fruit here follows the printed main text.

source.text: ውእተ፡ ጊዜ፡ አውሥአኒ፡ ሚካኤል፡ ፩እምነ፡ መላእክት፡ ቅዱሳን፡ ወክቡራን፡ እንዘ፡ ምስሌየ፡ ሀሎ፡ ውእቱ፡ ዘዲቤሆሙ።

translation.text: Then Michael, one of the holy and honored angels who was with me, answered me—he who was over them.[a]

footnotes.text: Michael is the subject. The closing expression says he was over them without naming the plural referent here; honored may also be rendered glorious. The following chapter supplies his speech, which is not imported.
